questions.question: In formal syllogism logic, what does the statement "Some A are B" guarantee?
options: At least one A is B, and definitely not all A are B
At least one A is B — it is still possible that all A are B
questions.rationale: "Some" only guarantees "at least one" in formal logic — it does not exclude the possibility that all A are B. Reading it as "not all" is one of the most common syllogism mistakes.

questions.question: If both given statements in a syllogism are of the form "Some A are B" and "Some B are C", what can be concluded about A and C?
questions.rationale: At least one universal (All/No) premise is required for any definite conclusion. Two particular ("Some") premises can combine in too many different Venn arrangements to guarantee anything about A and C.

questions.question: Statements: No teachers are students. All students are learners. Which conclusion definitely follows?
questions.rationale: Since all students are learners, and no teacher is a student, the student-learners are guaranteed not to be teachers — so at least some learners are not teachers.

questions.question: Two conclusions are: "All books are papers" and "Some books are not papers." What does the complementary pairs rule tell you about them?
options: At least one of the two must be true
questions.rationale: These two conclusions form a complementary pair — across every possible Venn arrangement, at least one of them must hold, so the answer always includes 'either I or II follows.'

questions.question: Statements: All A are B. All C are B. What can be concluded about 'Some A are C'?
options: It is only possible, never definite
No relationship can ever be inferred
questions.rationale: Both A and C being subsets of B doesn't guarantee they overlap with each other — 'Some A are C' is possible in some Venn arrangements but not guaranteed in all, so it is never a definite conclusion.

questions.question: Which premise combination can never yield a definite conclusion about the two end terms?
questions.rationale: Two negative premises (No + No) give no valid conclusion — knowing A excludes B and B excludes C tells you nothing definite about the relationship between A and C.

questions.question: How many different Venn diagram pictures can correctly represent 'All A are B'?
options: Only one — A entirely inside B
It cannot be pictured at all
questions.rationale: 'All A are B' has exactly one valid picture: circle A drawn completely inside circle B. 'Some A are B', by contrast, has two valid pictures.

questions.question: Statements: All pens are blue. No blue things are cheap. Conclusion: No pens are cheap. Does this follow?
questions.rationale: This is an All + No combination: all pens are blue, and no blue things are cheap, so no pens can be cheap either — a valid definite conclusion.

questions.question: Statements: Some doctors are teachers. Some teachers are students. Conclusion: Some doctors are students. Does this follow?
options: No, two 'Some' premises never guarantee a definite conclusion
Only if all doctors are also students
It follows only in reverse (some students are doctors)
questions.rationale: Some + Some is a particular-plus-particular combination, which can never guarantee a definite conclusion about the end terms — at least one universal (All/No) premise is required.

questions.question: Why must you treat every syllogism statement as true, even if it sounds false in real life?
options: Because the exam always uses false statements
Because syllogism logic evaluates whether conclusions follow IF the premises are true, regardless of real-world accuracy
Because real-world knowledge is always wrong
Because syllogism questions are never about real topics
questions.rationale: Syllogism reasoning tests whether a conclusion logically follows from the given premises, assuming they are true — importing real-world truth or falsity leads to incorrectly accepting or rejecting valid conclusions.
